extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials, policymakers, congressional staff, and administrative law practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS) recommendations and statements that provide formal guidance to federal agencies, Congress, and the judiciary on administrative procedure, rulemaking, adjudication, and related topics. The page lists adopted recommendations with short executive-summary text and metadata (project, recommendation number, adoption date, committee).

rubrics_metrics.name: ACUS recommendations — function and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: One of ACUS's primary statutory functions is to make recommendations for action by federal agencies, the President, Congress, and the Judicial Conference of the United States to improve administrative procedure. Adopted recommendations are published on the ACUS website and in the Federal Register. The Chair and ACUS staff undertake activities to encourage federal agencies to carry out recommendations adopted by ACUS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations are developed by committees of ACUS members, typically with the support of expert consultants and ACUS staff, and are adopted by the full membership at twice-yearly plenary sessions. (Metadata published with each recommendation includes project, recommendation number, adoption date, and committee.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements (ACUS)
rubrics_metrics.description: ACUS sometimes adopts “Statements,” which express the agency's views on a particular matter without making a formal recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements are developed through the same process as recommendations but typically set forth issues, conclusions from a study, or comments, rather than recommendations. ACUS has adopted 20 statements.

rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules adopted by federal agencies are generally subject to review in the federal courts. As the Administrative Conference has recognized, these tools 'hold out the promise of lowering the cost of completing government tasks and improving the quality, consistency, and predictability of agencies’ decisions.'
